questions.q:
Assertion (A): After 1008 Mahmud had easy access to the Indus plains and the lands beyond.
Reason (R): The Hindu Shahis, who had resisted earlier invasions, had now been overrun by the Ghaznavids.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. The Shahis had held the way in from the Khyber Pass side, so once they were overrun and Anandapala was overcome the route into the Indus plains lay open. R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Aman writes, 'In 1018 Mahmud sacked Mathura, and he was then already 58 years old.' Using the year and age of his death given in the chapter, show that this cannot be right, and say about how old he was in 1018.
questions.a: Mahmud died in 1030 at the age of 58. In 1018 he was 12 years younger, so about 58 - 12 = 46 years old (45 or 46, depending on his birthday). If he had been 58 in 1018, he would have been about 70 at his death, which the chapter does not say.
s: Recalls death in 1030 at the age of 58
Shows that 58 in 1018 would make him 70 in 1030, so the claim is impossible
States the age as about 46 (45 or 46 accepted) in 1018

questions.q:
A textbook committee is choosing two quotations about Mahmud for a classroom display. Quotation X, from a scholar who travelled with his army: 'The Hindu Shahiya dynasty is now extinct ... they never slackened in the ardent desire of doing that which is good and right.' Quotation Y, from his court historian: 'Wherever he went, Mahmud plundered and sacked the country until it was annihilated ... destroying their temples ... built mosques instead.'
(a) Name the scholar who wrote Quotation X and the region (now in Uzbekistan) he came from.
(b) What does Quotation X tell us about the writer's attitude, given where he stood?
(c) Which two aims of Mahmud does Quotation Y point to?
(d) A student proposes to display only Quotation Y and write 'Plunder was the only reason for the raids'. Using Quotation Y and what the chapter says about larger temples, judge this proposal.
questions.a: (a) Al-Biruni, from Khwarizm. (b) The writer, though in Mahmud's entourage, spoke of the defeated dynasty with respect. (c) Plunder and spreading his version of Islam (destroying temples and building mosques). (d) The proposal is weak. Larger temples held immense wealth from centuries of offerings, so plunder was a real motive, but Quotation Y itself speaks of destroying temples and building mosques, pointing to spreading Islam. The word 'only' is therefore too strong.
s: Part (a): al-Biruni, from Khwarizm
Part (b): respect for the defeated dynasty from a writer on the conqueror's side
Part (c): plunder and spreading his version of Islam
Part (d): uses Quotation Y and the wealth of larger temples to reject 'only'

questions.q: Meena says, 'The Hindu Shahis lost to the Ghaznavids, so their long resistance changed nothing.' Which reply uses the chapter's reasoning best?
questions.a: It mattered: they held the Khyber Pass, so Mahmud had no easy way into the Indus plains until he overran them
o: It mattered: they held the Khyber Pass, so Mahmud had no easy way into the Indus plains until he overran them
It failed completely because Anandapala was beaten at the Khyber Pass in the very first year of Mahmud's campaigns
It mattered because the Shahis held Somnath, the seaport that Mahmud could not reach until 1026
It changed nothing, since Mahmud then ruled the Gangetic plains from a permanent base at Mathura

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT stated in the chapter about Mahmud of Ghazni's campaigns?
questions.a: The chapter says he did not try to set up a permanent base in India beyond Punjab, so he did not rule the Gangetic plains from Mathura. The other three are given in the text.
o: He ruled the Ganga plains from a new capital, Mathura
He returned to Ghazni with huge booty after each campaign
His army used horse-mounted archers in daring attacks
The Chandellas of central India resisted him strongly

questions.q:
Using the dates of Mahmud's career given in the chapter, match each gap in Column A with its length in Column B.
Column A: 1. Overcoming Anandapala to the sack of Mathura  2. The sack of Mathura to the destruction of Somnath  3. The destruction of Somnath to Mahmud's death  4. Overcoming Anandapala to Mahmud's death
Column B: a. 4 years  b. 8 years  c. 22 years  d. 10 years
questions.a: 1-d, 2-b, 3-a, 4-c. Anandapala was overcome in 1008, Mathura sacked in 1018, Somnath destroyed in 1026 and Mahmud died in 1030, so the gaps are 10, 8, 4 and 22 years.

questions.q: Dev says, 'This chapter should skip the destruction and killing of Mahmud's raids so that nobody feels bad.' Using the 'word of caution' at the start of the chapter's account, do you agree?
questions.a: No. The chapter says history has often recorded war and destruction more than peace, and that it is better to face dark periods and analyse them to understand what made them possible and help avoid recurrence. It also adds that it is wrong to hold anyone responsible today for past events.
s: Verdict: disagrees, the darker periods should be faced
Reason: analysing them shows what made them possible and helps avoid recurrence
Adds that nobody today is to be held responsible for past events

questions.q: (a) Al-Utbi, Mahmud's court historian, wrote that even 'the pens of all writers and the pencils of all painters' could not describe the beauty of the temple at Mathura, which Mahmud then destroyed. What does this tell a reader about how to use him as a source? (b) After Mathura, which city did Mahmud proceed to, and whom did he take by surprise there?
questions.a: (a) He wrote from inside Mahmud's court, so the same writer can admire the temple and record its destruction; his facts about the campaign are useful, but the reader must remember whose side he wrote from. (b) Kannauj, where he took one of the last Pratihara rulers by surprise.
s: reads the source as written from Mahmud's court, admiration and destruction together
names Kannauj and the Pratihara ruler taken by surprise

questions.q: True or False: Because Mahmud of Ghazni took the title 'sultan', he founded the Delhi Sultanate. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. 'Sultan' is an Arabic word meaning authority or power, and in the Muslim world it came to mean a sovereign ruler. Taking it did not make Mahmud ruler of Delhi: he raided and returned to Ghazni; the Delhi Sultanate comes later (Grade 8), after Muhammad Ghuri's generals.
s: verdict: False
corrects it: the title only means authority or power, and Mahmud set up no base in India

questions.q: 'Mahmud's campaigns met resistance only from the Hindu Shahis.' Justify or refute this statement using at least three examples from the chapter.
questions.a: The statement is false. The Hindu Shahis did resist, and Anandapala fought a long battle in 1008 with help from several north Indian rulers. But the Chandellas of central India also resisted strongly and Mahmud was close to defeat a few times, and at Somnath the locals resisted strongly and his army suffered severe losses before he gained the upper hand. So resistance came from several quarters; Mahmud's rapid marches and daring cavalry with mounted archers were ultimately decisive.
s: Verdict: refutes the statement as too narrow
The Shahis' long battle in 1008 with support from other rulers
The Chandellas' strong resistance and Mahmud being close to defeat
Somnath: strong local resistance and severe losses to his army
Concludes that rapid marches and cavalry still decided the outcome

questions.q: The chapter's timeline puts the sack of Mathura in 1018 and the destruction of the Somnath temple in 1026, so Mahmud's two raids were ___ years apart.

(a) Name the dynasty that controlled the Khyber Pass before the Ghaznavids overran it, and say what else the pass was used for, apart from invasions, for at least 2,500 years. (b) A Ghaznavid ruler wants to reach the Indus plains from Ghazni. Why must he first deal with that dynasty?
questions.a: (a) The Hindu Shahis; the pass was a major trade route connecting the Subcontinent to Central Asia and the route Buddhist scholars and monks travelled. (b) The Shahis held the pass through which invaders entered the Subcontinent, so the way into the Indus plains lay through their territory; the Ghaznavids had to overrun them first.
s: Part (a): Hindu Shahis, and the pass as a trade route and a route for Buddhist scholars and monks
Part (b): invaders entered through this pass, so controlling it made resistance count

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the Ghaznavid invasions.
1. Mahmud conducted 17 campaigns in India.
2. In 1008 Anandapala defeated Mahmud because several rulers of north India helped him.
3. Salar Masud, according to oral history and a 17th-century chronicle, fell in battle against Suheldev at Bahraich.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: Mahmud overcame Anandapala in 1008 despite the help Anandapala received from other north Indian rulers.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Describe how Mahmud of Ghazni overcame the Hindu Shahis and then raided deeper into India, and explain why the chapter treats his campaigns as raids and not as the founding of a lasting rule.
questions.a: The Shahis held the Khyber Pass and resisted with the help of other Indian rulers. Mahmud defeated Jayapala and, in 1008, Jayapala's son Anandapala after a long battle in northern Punjab, which opened the Indus plains. He sacked Mathura in 1018, looted Kannauj and destroyed Somnath in 1026. In all he made 17 campaigns and returned to Ghazni with booty each time. He did not attempt a permanent base beyond Punjab, so the campaigns were raids.
s: Shahis, the Khyber Pass and the defeat of Jayapala
1008 victory over Anandapala despite help from other rulers
Mathura, Kannauj and Somnath named with the kind of damage done
17 campaigns, each ending with a return to Ghazni with booty
No permanent base beyond Punjab, so raids and not lasting rule

questions.q: (a) Give two features of Mahmud's army that were ultimately decisive even when he met strong resistance. (b) The chapter says he was close to defeat on a few occasions and names a central Indian dynasty that resisted him strongly. Name it, and say why this fact weakens the claim that his army could not be stopped.
questions.a: (a) Rapid marches and daring cavalry attacks with archers on horseback. (b) The Chandellas; if he came close to defeat on a few occasions, his success was not automatic, so the claim is too strong.
s: two features: rapid marches and mounted archers or cavalry
Chandellas, and the near-defeats show success was not certain

questions.q: (a) Salar Masud's fall at Bahraich is known only from oral history and a 17th-century Muslim chronicle. If that chronicle was written in 1601 or later, what is the least number of years after Mahmud's death in 1030 that it was written? (b) Why should a historian be careful with such a source?
questions.a: (a) 1601 - 1030 = 571 years at least. (b) It was written long after the events, so details may have changed in retelling; the chapter itself says 'according to' these sources, so they need support from other evidence.
s: 571 years from 1601 - 1030
a source written centuries later needs checking against other evidence

questions.q: Nisha reads that a ruler fought a campaign every few years, took back wealth and prisoners to his own capital each time, and set up no lasting base beyond one province. Which description from the chapter fits him best?
questions.a: Mahmud returned to Ghazni with booty after each of 17 campaigns and did not build a base beyond Punjab, which makes his campaigns repeated raids. Muhammad Ghuri is the contrast: he sought territorial conquest and left commanders behind.
o: Mahmud of Ghazni, whose campaigns were repeated raids
Muhammad Ghuri, who left Aibak to rule Delhi
Prithviraj III, who held Delhi and Ajmer for his own kingdom
Bakhtiyar Khilji, who took Bihar and Bengal for the Ghurids

questions.q:
The history club of a Pune school is making a timeline poster on Mahmud's campaigns. The draft entries read: 'A long battle in northern Punjab, 1008'; 'A wealthy city of western Uttar Pradesh whose temple overlooked it, 1018, followed by Kannauj'; 'A bustling seaport of Saurashtra, 1026'; 'Died at Ghazni aged 58, 1030'.
(a) Name the city of the second entry and the temple of the third.
(b) Which dynasty did Mahmud overcome in the first entry, and what did that victory give him?
(c) Name two things, besides plunder of treasure, that his campaigns involved.
(d) The club must choose a title: 'The Ghaznavid Raids' or 'The Ghaznavid Conquest'. Decide which title the entries and one fact in the chapter support better, and say why the other fits less well.
questions.a: (a) Mathura; the Somnath (Somanatha Shiva) temple. (b) The Hindu Shahis (Anandapala, son of Jayapala); the victory gave him easy access to the Indus plains and beyond. (c) Destruction of temples, killing of tens of thousands of civilians and capture of prisoners, including children, sold on slave markets of Central Asia. (d) 'Raids' fits better: he returned to Ghazni after each of 17 campaigns and set up no permanent base beyond Punjab. 'Conquest' fits only the overrunning of the Shahis, so it overstates the rest.
s: Part (a): Mathura and the Somnath temple
Part (b): Hindu Shahis, and easy access to the Indus plains
Part (c): two of destruction, slaughter of civilians, capture and sale of prisoners
Part (d): prefers Raids with the return-to-Ghazni / no-base fact and explains why Conquest fits less

questions.q: Historians have debated why Mahmud destroyed temples. Explain the debate by giving one point each from: what he did not do in India, what larger temples held, and what a contemporary writer noted.
questions.a: He did not try to set up a permanent base beyond Punjab, so many historians suggest plunder was the chief reason. Larger temples held immense wealth built up from devotees' offerings, so they were prime targets. But al-Utbi noted that he destroyed temples and built mosques, which shows Mahmud was also keen to spread his version of Islam.
s: No permanent base beyond Punjab, so plunder is suggested
Large temples held immense wealth from offerings and were prime targets
Al-Utbi's remark shows the aim of spreading his version of Islam

questions.q: A visitor to a museum reads that a Persian scholar who travelled with Mahmud wrote of the Hindu Shahis: 'in all their grandeur, they never slackened in the ardent desire of doing that which is good and right'. What can be concluded from this?
questions.a: A man from the invader's own entourage could write with respect about the defeated dynasty. He also calls the house extinct, so it does not show that the Shahis still ruled.
o: Even a writer in the conqueror's camp praised the Shahis
The writer was a minister who served the Hindu Shahi court
The Hindu Shahis were still ruling Punjab when he wrote this
The writer composed this remark before Jayapala was defeated

questions.q: True or False: Al-Biruni wrote his encyclopaedic survey of India in Sanskrit, since he had learned Sanskrit to read Indian texts. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. He learned Sanskrit to read Indian texts and talk with scholars, but the chapter says he wrote prolifically in Arabic and Persian, so his survey was not written in Sanskrit.
s: verdict: False
corrects it: Sanskrit was a language he learned for reading; he wrote in Arabic and Persian

questions.q:
A school magazine in Lucknow is preparing a page on a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who came to India around 1017 with an army. The editor has two pieces of material: his encyclopaedic survey of India, and one sentence in which he says that the ruler he accompanied 'utterly ruined the prosperity of the country' and that Indian sciences 'fled to places which our hand cannot yet reach'. She must choose one heading for the page: 'An enemy's account of India', 'A scholar who studied India and recorded its losses', or 'A silent witness of the raids'.
(a) Name the scholar and the ruler he accompanied.
(b) Name two things he did to learn about India before writing the survey.
(c) What did he note about the effect of the ruler's campaigns, and where did the sciences go?
(d) Choose one heading and justify it using the survey and the sentence; say why one other heading fits less well.
questions.a: (a) Al-Biruni and Mahmud of Ghazni. (b) Any two of: learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts, conversed with Indian scholars. (c) He noted that Mahmud ruined the country's prosperity and that Indian sciences retired far from the conquered parts to places such as Kashmir and Varanasi. (d) 'A scholar who studied India and recorded its losses' fits best: the survey shows serious study of Indian religion, philosophy, sciences and more, and the sentence shows he openly recorded the damage. 'Enemy's account' ignores the survey and his respect for the Shahis; 'silent witness' is wrong because he wrote at length and spoke plainly.
s: Part (a): al-Biruni and Mahmud of Ghazni
Part (b): two of learning Sanskrit, reading texts, talking with scholars
Part (c): ruined prosperity; sciences moved to Kashmir, Varanasi and other places
Part (d): picks the scholar heading, justifies with survey and sentence, and rejects one other

questions.q: Describe three signs from the chapter that Bhaskaracharya's influence was long-lasting and reached beyond his own time.
questions.a: Many later scholars wrote commentaries on his works. Several were translated into Persian in the Mughal period. Europe took a few centuries to rediscover some of his pioneering techniques.
s: Later commentaries by many scholars
Persian translations in the Mughal period
Europe's rediscovery of some techniques a few centuries later

questions.q: Write a riddle in the style of Lilavati about peacocks in a Jaipur fort garden whose answer is a whole number, and solve it.
questions.a: Any valid riddle that can be solved, for example: 'A third of the peacocks were dancing, a sixth sat on the wall, and 9 were drinking at the fountain. How many peacocks?' A third and a sixth make a half, so 9 is the other half and the flock is 18.
s: A riddle in a story or verse style with clear numbers
The riddle can be solved to a whole number
The working and the final answer are correct

questions.q: Which of the following was NOT done by al-Biruni, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Lilavati was written by Bhaskaracharya, born in 1114, while al-Biruni came to India around 1017. The other three are credited to al-Biruni.
o: Writing the book Lilavati with riddles for students
Translating Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic
Comparing Indian achievements with Greek and Islamic ones
Compiling the work of Aryabhata and Brahmagupta

questions.q: Zoya is asked which of Bhaskaracharya's works is called the 'Crown of Treatises on Mathematical Astronomy'. She first answers Lilavati. What should she say, and why is her first answer wrong?
questions.a: Siddhantashiromani; Lilavati teaches basic mathematics through lively riddles
o: Siddhantashiromani; Lilavati teaches basic mathematics through lively riddles
Bijaganita; Lilavati is the work that deals with advanced algebra and equations
Lilavati is right, because it deals with advanced astronomical calculations for scholars
Yogasutras; Lilavati was written by al-Biruni after he reached India around 1017

questions.q: A scholar from Khwarizm reaches India around 1017 and wants to understand Indian astronomy from its own books. What did al-Biruni do, according to the chapter?
questions.a: He learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and talked with Indian scholars. The Persian translations of Bhaskaracharya came in the Mughal period, and Lilavati was composed long after 1017.
o: Learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and talked with scholars
Read a Persian translation of Lilavati from Mahmud's library
Asked Bhaskaracharya to explain Siddhantashiromani to him
Relied on Greek summaries and wrote without Indian books

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bhaskaracharya's writings were favourite texts of students for centuries.
Reason (R): Siddhantashiromani deals with advanced astronomical calculations.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true. But the reason does not explain the assertion: the chapter says the works were favourites because of their examples, clear explanations, demonstrations and proofs, and his gift for poetry.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Kiran wants to teach fractions to her Class 7 friends through verse riddles about elephants and lotus ponds, the way a 12th-century scholar did. Which work should she study as her model?
questions.a: Lilavati uses lively riddles and problems to teach basic mathematics, with the elephant-herd problem as an example. Bijaganita is advanced algebra and Siddhantashiromani is astronomy.
o: Lilavati
Bijaganita
Siddhantashiromani
Yogasutras

questions.q: 'Al-Biruni came to India with Mahmud's army, yet he studied India seriously.' Support this statement with five points from the chapter.
questions.a: He was a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who accompanied Mahmud around 1017. Even so, he learned Sanskrit, read Indian texts and conversed with Indian scholars. His encyclopaedic survey covered Indian religion, philosophy, literature, geography and sciences and compared them with Greek and Islamic traditions. He compiled the work of Aryabhata, Varahamihira and Brahmagupta and translated Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic. He also recorded candidly how Mahmud's campaigns had harmed India's sciences.
s: His background: a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who accompanied Mahmud around 1017
Learning Sanskrit, reading texts and talking with Indian scholars
The survey and its comparison with Greek and Islamic traditions
Compiling Indian mathematics and astronomy and translating the Yogasutras
Recording how Mahmud's campaigns affected Indian sciences

questions.q: The chapter gives this Lilavati problem: of a herd of elephants, half and one-third of the half went into a cave; one-sixth and one-seventh of one-sixth drank at a river; one-eighth and one-ninth of one-eighth sported in a pond; and the king of the elephants led three female elephants. (a) What fraction of the herd is in the cave, at the river and in the pond together? (b) Taking the king and the three female elephants (4 elephants) as the rest of the herd, how many elephants were there?
questions.a: (a) Cave 2/3, river 4/21, pond 5/36; together 251/252 of the herd. (b) The remaining 1/252 of the herd is 4 elephants, so the herd is 4 x 252 = 1008 elephants.
s: adds the three fractions to 251/252
the remaining 1/252 equals 4 elephants, so 1008

questions.q: Imran writes, 'Because al-Biruni worked in Persian, the Persian translations of Bhaskaracharya's works were made in the Ghaznavid age.' Which correction is supported by the chapter?
questions.a: Several were translated into Persian in the Mughal period, long after Bhaskaracharya
o: Several were translated into Persian in the Mughal period, long after Bhaskaracharya
They were translated into Persian by the Hoysala court, soon after Bhaskaracharya wrote
They were never translated, and only the Yogasutras reached Persian readers
They were translated into Arabic by al-Biruni when he accompanied Mahmud around 1017

questions.q: (a) Al-Biruni translated Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic. Which two skills, both mentioned in the chapter, did this task need? (b) Why does a translation like this matter for readers who know only Arabic?
questions.a: (a) He had learned Sanskrit to read Indian texts and he wrote in Arabic. (b) It makes a classic Indian text on yoga available to readers who cannot read Sanskrit, so Indian ideas travel beyond the Subcontinent.
s: Sanskrit learned and Arabic writing
translation opens Indian knowledge to readers of another language

questions.q: A student claims that al-Biruni's survey of India only copied what Indian books said. Using the chapter, give two reasons why the claim is too strong.
questions.a: He often compared Indian intellectual achievements with Greek and Islamic traditions, and he also conversed with Indian scholars and noted the impact of Mahmud's campaigns on Indian sciences. These show comparison and judgement, not copying alone.
s: comparison with Greek and Islamic traditions
conversation with scholars or his own note on the campaigns' impact

questions.q: Al-Biruni came to India around 1017 and Bhaskaracharya was born in 1114, so Bhaskaracharya was born ___ years after al-Biruni's visit.
Ritu says, 'Al-Biruni's remark shows that Indian sciences retreated from the parts Mahmud conquered, but it does not show that Indian science came to an end.' Is she right? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Al-Biruni said the sciences retired from the conquered parts to places such as Kashmir and Varanasi, so they moved rather than ended. The chapter adds that scientific knowledge declined in north India only a little later and continued to flourish in other regions, as in Bhaskaracharya (born 1114), whose Lilavati dates to about 1150. Her claim is right as stated; it would be wrong only if stretched to 'all Indian science continued everywhere'.
s: Verdict: agrees, the sciences moved and did not end
Al-Biruni's own words name Kashmir and Varanasi
Bhaskaracharya as evidence of continued flourishing, and the limit of the claim

questions.q: (a) The chapter's timeline dates Bhaskaracharya's Lilavati to 1150 and says he was born in 1114. How old was he when it was composed? (b) The chapter says scientific knowledge declined in north India a little later but kept flourishing elsewhere. Which present-day region is given as his probable birthplace, and why does it support that statement?
questions.a: (a) 1150 - 1114 = 36 years old. (b) Probably present-day Maharashtra; a great mathematician working there shows science flourished outside north India.
s: 36 years from 1150 - 1114
Maharashtra, outside the north where science continued

questions.q: Compare al-Biruni and Bhaskaracharya on their homeland, their languages, their main works and what each contributed to the learning of the age.
questions.a: Al-Biruni was a Persian scholar from Khwarizm who wrote in Arabic and Persian; Bhaskaracharya was born in 1114, probably in present-day Maharashtra, and wrote in Sanskrit. Al-Biruni's main work was a survey of India; Bhaskaracharya's were Lilavati, Bijaganita and Siddhantashiromani. Al-Biruni gathered, compared and translated existing knowledge, while Bhaskaracharya advanced mathematics and astronomy with pioneering techniques in works that students loved for centuries.
s: Homeland of each scholar
Language of writing for each
Main works of al-Biruni
Main works of Bhaskaracharya
Contrast between recording and comparing existing knowledge, and advancing it

questions.q:
Read the following statements about two scholars of the age.
1. Al-Biruni was a mathematician, astronomer, geographer, historian and linguist.
2. He translated Patanjali's Yogasutras into Arabic.
3. Bhaskaracharya was born in 1114, probably in present-day Maharashtra.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are from the chapter: al-Biruni's many fields, his Arabic translation of the Yogasutras and Bhaskaracharya's birth year and probable birthplace.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only

questions.q:
A maths club in Nagpur has 22 members and is studying a 12th-century Sanskrit book that teaches basic mathematics through lively riddles. For next term it can buy only one more work by the same author. A survey shows that 14 members want to go on to more advanced algebra and 5 members want to learn advanced astronomical calculations; the other 3 have no preference.
(a) Name the book the club is studying and its author.
(b) Name the author's other two famous works and say what each deals with.
(c) Several of these works were translated into Persian in a later period. Name the period and say what it shows about the author.
(d) Which work should the club buy? Decide using the survey figures and the subject of each work.
questions.a: (a) Lilavati by Bhaskaracharya. (b) Bijaganita, on more advanced algebra; and Siddhantashiromani ('Crown of Treatises on Mathematical Astronomy'), on advanced astronomical calculations. (c) The Mughal period; it shows his influence was long-lasting in India and beyond. (d) Bijaganita: 14 of 22 members (the majority) want advanced algebra, against only 5 for astronomy, and Bijaganita is the work on advanced algebra.
s: Part (a): Lilavati by Bhaskaracharya
Part (b): Bijaganita (advanced algebra) and Siddhantashiromani (astronomical calculations)
Part (c): Mughal period, showing long-lasting influence
Part (d): Bijaganita, justified by 14 of 22 against 5 and the work's subject

questions.q: The chapter says that while north India bore the brunt of the Ghaznavid raids, the scene in eastern India was 'very different'. Using the two eastern dynasties named in the chapter's account, explain how it was different.
questions.a: In eastern India the chapter describes the rise and flourishing of local dynasties rather than Ghaznavid raids. The Senas became the dominant power in Bengal after the Palas, with their capital at Nadiya. The Eastern Gangas of Kalinga became one of the most stable powers of eastern India by the end of the 12th century, and began the Puri and Konark temples.
s: North India faced the raids, but the chapter's eastern story is of local dynasties
The Senas became dominant in Bengal after the Palas
The Eastern Gangas as a stable power that began major temples

questions.q: True or False: Since the Eastern Gangas had matrimonial alliances with the Cholas, the two dynasties never fought each other. Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the Eastern Gangas had matrimonial alliances with the Cholas, yet also clashed with them a few times, so a marriage alliance did not rule out war.
s: verdict: False
corrects it: they clashed with the Cholas a few times despite the alliances

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Senas are remembered as patrons of Hindu thought and literature.
Reason (R): Jayadeva, the author of the Gitagovindam, was hosted by the Palas.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true because the Senas hosted poets such as Jayadeva. R is false because Jayadeva was hosted by the Senas, while the Palas patronised Buddhist institutions.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A quiz-setter wants a clue that fits the Senas of Bengal and not their predecessors. Which clue works?
questions.a: Its court hosted Jayadeva, whose Gitagovindam tells of Krishna and Radha

questions.q:
Using the dates in the chapter, match each gap in Column A with its length in Column B.
Column A: 1. Defeat at Mount Abu (1178) to the Second Battle of Tarain (1192)  2. Second Battle of Tarain to Bakhtiyar's defeat in Kamarupa (1205)  3. First Battle of Tarain (1191) to the Second  4. Defeat at Mount Abu to the deaths of Muhammad Ghuri and Bakhtiyar Khilji (1206)
Column B: a. 1 year  b. 13 years  c. 14 years  d. 28 years
In 1203-04 a Sena minister at Nadiya hears that Bakhtiyar Khilji's force is approaching. Which outcome does the chapter record?
questions.a: He caught the Sena ruler unaware, ending Sena control over much of Bengal
o: He caught the Sena ruler unaware, ending Sena control over much of Bengal
He was driven off from Nadiya by the Senas and fled with only a handful of men
He made the Senas his vassals and left them in charge of Bengal and Bihar
He destroyed the Sena capital and was himself defeated at Mount Abu soon after

questions.q: A tour guide at Patan in Gujarat says, 'The Chaulukyas, also called Solanki, who ruled from Anahilavada, are just the same as the Chalukya dynasty of the Deccan.' What does the chapter say?
questions.a: They are distinct dynasties; the Chaulukyas ruled parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan
o: They are distinct dynasties; the Chaulukyas ruled parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan
They are the same dynasty, which moved its capital from Kalyani in the Deccan to Patan in Gujarat
The Chaulukyas ruled the Deccan from Kalyani, and the Chalukyas ruled parts of Gujarat and Rajasthan
The Chaulukyas were a branch of the Chahamanas, who ruled from Ajayameru, today's Ajmer, in Rajasthan

questions.q: A student says, 'The name Delhi was first given to the city by the Ghurids after Muhammad Ghuri captured it.' Using the chapter, give two points that correct her.
questions.a: Delhi was already a flourishing city under the Chahamanas, whose inscriptions called it 'Dhillika'; that name was later shortened to 'Dhilli' and finally became 'Delhi'. So the name grew out of an older name rather than being given at the Ghurid capture.
s: Chahamana inscriptions already call it Dhillika
the name was shortened to Dhilli and evolved into Delhi over time

questions.q:
A history class studies this passage, written by a chronicler about 60 years after a commander's campaign through Bihar: 'The greater number of the inhabitants of that place were Brahmans, and all those Brahmans had their heads shaven; and they were all slain. There were a great number of books there ... the whole of that fortress and city was a college, and in their tongue they call a college bihar.' A student argues the passage should be thrown out since it was written long afterwards and calls the place a fortress.
(a) Name the commander whose campaign is described and the famous university nearby.
(b) Whom do the shaven heads and the word 'bihar' really point to?
(c) State two facts about that university's library given in the chapter.
(d) Judge the student's suggestion.
questions.a: (a) Bakhtiyar Khilji; Nalanda. (b) Buddhist monks and a vihara, a monastery. (c) Its library was spread over three multi-storey buildings and held lakhs of manuscripts; it is said to have burned for months. (d) The passage should not simply be thrown out. It is a later account, so it should be read with care and checked against other evidence, but its clues (books, shaven heads, 'bihar') fit a monastery-university, and the chapter's other facts support the picture of destruction.
s: Part (a): Bakhtiyar Khilji and Nalanda
Part (b): Buddhist monks and a vihara
Part (c): two library facts
Part (d): reasoned judgement, reading with care instead of rejecting it

questions.q:
Students on a school trip to Taraori in Haryana are told that two battles were fought there within about a year. In the first, the king of a Rajput dynasty of Rajasthan won. In the second, the larger army of a sultan from Ghur won, and the defeated king was executed. The students must design a poster for the section 'A turning point: the Ghurids in India', on the theme 'how the Ghurids gained a lasting hold on north India'.
(a) Name the two rulers and the years of the battles.
(b) Name the dynasty of the first ruler and its capital.
(c) What did the winner do with Delhi and whom did he leave behind to hold his gains?
(d) Which should be the lead event for this theme, the Second Battle of Tarain or Bakhtiyar Khilji's campaign in Bihar and Bengal? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Prithviraj III (1191) and Muhammad Ghuri (1192). (b) The Chahamanas (Chauhans), with capital Ajayameru (Ajmer). (c) He captured Delhi and left trusted commanders such as Qutb-ud-din Aibak. (d) The Second Battle of Tarain: it opened the way to Delhi, and since Muhammad, unlike Mahmud, sought territorial conquest and left commanders to consolidate, it started the lasting hold. Bakhtiyar's campaign is important for the destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila, but it came later and its main result in the chapter is the decline of Buddhism, not the first hold on north India.
s: Part (a): Prithviraj III in 1191 and Muhammad Ghuri in 1192
Part (b): Chahamanas and Ajayameru
Part (c): captured Delhi and left commanders such as Aibak
Part (d): Second Battle of Tarain with the territorial-conquest reasoning, and why the other event fits the theme less

questions.q: Compare Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad Ghuri in terms of their aims, methods and results for India, and analyse how their aims shaped the outcomes of their campaigns.
questions.a: Mahmud made repeated raids from Afghanistan, took plunder and withdrew each time, and did not try to set up a base beyond Punjab. Muhammad sought territorial conquest. He captured Delhi and left trusted commanders, such as Aibak, to consolidate his gains. Aibak later founded the Delhi Sultanate and Bakhtiyar Khilji conquered Bihar and Bengal. So Mahmud's aim left plunder and destruction but no lasting rule, while Muhammad's aim of control led to a lasting political presence in north India.
s: Mahmud's aim: repeated raids and plunder
Muhammad's aim: territorial conquest
Commanders left behind, such as Aibak, and what they did
Mahmud left no lasting base beyond Punjab, Muhammad's gains lasted
Links aim to outcome

questions.q: Describe how Bakhtiyar Khilji's campaigns changed eastern India, giving the places, the results and his defeat in Kamarupa.
questions.a: As Aibak's army commander he conducted campaigns in eastern India from the end of the 12th century and conquered Bihar and Bengal. On the way he destroyed large Buddhist monasteries and universities such as Nalanda and Vikramashila, took huge booty and slaughtered large numbers of monks, hastening Buddhism's decline. Around 1203-04 he caught the Sena ruler unaware at Nadiya, ending Sena control over much of Bengal. In 1205 he was defeated in Kamarupa, where the local population destroyed food and fodder and starved his army. He was assassinated in 1206.
s: Aibak's commander conquering Bihar and Bengal
Destruction of Nalanda and Vikramashila
Nadiya and the end of Sena control
Defeat in Kamarupa in 1205 and how it happened
Death in 1206

questions.q: A pupil summarises: 'After Prithviraj III defeated him in 1191, Muhammad Ghuri gave up India for good.' Which correction fits the chapter?
questions.a: Within a year he returned with a larger army and won the Second Battle of Tarain
o: Within a year he returned with a larger army and won the Second Battle of Tarain
He lost again at Tarain in 1192 and Prithviraj III executed him on the battlefield
He accepted Prithviraj III's rule and was made the governor of the city of Delhi
He returned in 1178 and defeated Mularaja II at the foot of Mount Abu this time

questions.q: A pupil writes, 'Bakhtiyar Khilji's Tibet expedition of 1205 failed because the Tibetan army beat him in open battle in Tibet.' Do you agree? Use the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. The expedition did fail: Bakhtiyar escaped with only a handful of men and returned to Bengal much weakened. But the chapter places the setback on the way, in Kamarupa in 1205, where the local ruler's forces inflicted severe losses and the local population destroyed food and fodder, starving the army. He never fought the Tibetans in Tibet.
s: Verdict: partly right, the failure is correct
Failure shown: handful of men escaped, returned to Bengal weakened
Correction: the losses came in Kamarupa, from the local ruler's forces and the starving of the army, not in Tibet

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column A with the item in Column B that fits it.
Column A: 1. A reader wants a guide to royal life that stresses the duties of kings  2. A devotee seeks a school that sees the world and souls as real and stresses surrender to the divine  3. People of every caste and creed wish to discuss morals and religion in one pavilion  4. A pilgrim wants a Cambodian temple first dedicated to Vishnu with Ramayana reliefs
Column B: a. Anubhava Mandapa  b. Angkor Wat  c. Manasollasa  d. vishishtadvaita vedanta
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b. Manasollasa is the guide to royal life, vishishtadvaita is Ramanuja's school, the Anubhava Mandapa was Basava's open pavilion, and Angkor Wat was first dedicated to Vishnu. The wrong pairings swap the two thinkers' contributions or the two buildings.

questions.q: What is vishishtadvaita vedanta? Say whose school it challenged and what it emphasises for liberation.
questions.a: It is the school developed by Ramanujacharya that sees the world and individual souls as real. It challenged Adi Shankaracharya's advaita vedanta, and emphasises bhakti and surrender to the divine as the path to liberation.
s: The school sees the world and individual souls as real, developed by Ramanuja
Challenged advaita and stresses bhakti and surrender

questions.q: Archaeologists find coins and pottery from China and Southeast Asia at many sites on India's west coast, which had seaports and shipyards. A student concludes in her notes. Which conclusion matches the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says India's trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing despite political disturbances, while agriculture remained the mainstay of the economy. The other options are look-alikes: that trade replaced agriculture, that trade fell everywhere because the north was disturbed, or that only the Cholas traded overseas.
o: Overseas trade kept growing, though agriculture stayed the mainstay
Trade with China and Southeast Asia had replaced agriculture as the mainstay
Trade declined in the north and so declined everywhere
Only the Cholas traded overseas; other regions did not

questions.q:
A Hyderabad school's value-education club studies photographs of two huge modern statues of 12th-century south Indian thinkers. One was a royal minister at a Deccan court who gave up his post; the other was a philosopher-saint who challenged the dominant school of his time. A student says, 'These two were opposed to each other, because one was a reformer and the other a philosopher.'
(a) Name the minister, his town and the movement he founded.
(b) Name the philosopher-saint and the school he developed.
(c) Which dominant school did the philosopher-saint challenge, and what did the minister's movement reject?
(d) Judge the student's statement using what the chapter says both thinkers did for spirituality in south India.
questions.a: (a) Basaveshwara (Basavanna) at Kalyani, now Basavakalyana; the Lingayat movement. (b) Ramanujacharya; vishishtadvaita vedanta. (c) Adi Shankaracharya's advaita vedanta; caste distinctions and ritualism. (d) The statement is not supported. The chapter says both thinker-saints helped make spirituality more personal and accessible and broke down some existing social barriers; they worked differently (philosophy and bhakti versus rejecting caste and ritualism) but toward similar ends, and the chapter does not set them against each other.
s: Part (a): Basaveshwara, Kalyani, Lingayat movement
Part (b): Ramanujacharya and vishishtadvaita vedanta
Part (c): advaita vedanta challenged; caste distinctions and ritualism rejected
Part (d): rejects 'opposed' using the shared effect on spirituality and social barriers

questions.q: Someshvara III's Manasollasa and Bhoja's Samarangana Sutradhara both touch on architecture. (a) Which of the two is described as a guide to royal life and governance with emphasis on the duties of kings? (b) Name two other subjects, besides architecture, that the Manasollasa covers.
questions.a: (a) The Manasollasa, by the Chalukya ruler Someshvara III in the 12th century. (b) Any two of astronomy, music, medicine, cooking and games.
s: Manasollasa named as the guide stressing the duties of kings
two other subjects from astronomy, music, medicine, cooking, games

questions.q: Explain how the Lingayat movement and the Anubhava Mandapa tried to reduce social barriers.
questions.a: Basaveshwara left a minister's post to found the Lingayat movement, which rejected caste distinctions and ritualism and taught personal devotion and dedicated work. He looked at a person's inner value, not rank, and promoted equal spiritual potential. At the Anubhava Mandapa men and women of every background could meet and discuss life, morals and religion.
s: Rejected caste distinctions and ritualism, teaching personal devotion
Judged people by inner value and equal spiritual potential of men and women
The Anubhava Mandapa as a meeting place for all backgrounds

questions.q: Give two changes and two continuities from the 11th and 12th centuries, and decide whether 'turning point' is a fair title for the period, giving reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Changes: the military campaigns by Turkic invaders and the start of foreign rule in parts of north India, with plunder and destruction of temples, cities and centres of learning; and the spread of Islam as a new creed in India's religious landscape. Continuities: large parts of northern India and all of south India stayed outside the invaders' hold, and trade, merchant guilds, art, literature and learning continued, with Indian culture travelling to Southeast Asia and China. Verdict: 'turning point' is fair, since the balance of power altered profoundly in the north, but it must not be stretched to mean everything changed, as the chapter's lesson is resilience and the enduring power of knowledge, learning and creativity.
s: First change, such as the Turkic campaigns and the start of foreign rule in the north
Second change, such as destruction of centres of learning or the spread of Islam
First continuity, such as the south and large parts of the north outside the invaders' hold
Second continuity, such as trade, guilds, art and literature carrying on
Verdict on the title with a reason that weighs change against continuity

questions.q: 'Despite wars, the economy and cultural life of the 11th and 12th centuries flourished.' Justify this statement with points on farming, trade, temples, literature and thinkers.
questions.a: Agriculture remained the mainstay, with rice and barley, saffron, spices, ginger, wheat and cotton in different regions, and rulers built irrigation works. Trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing, with coins and pottery found on the west coast, seaports, shipyards and powerful guilds. Large temples were built, including those at Khajuraho by the Chandellas. Literature included Bhoja's works and Someshvara III's Manasollasa. Thinkers such as Ramanuja and Basaveshwara shaped south Indian culture.
s: Agriculture, crops and irrigation
Overseas trade, seaports, shipyards and guilds
Temples such as those at Khajuraho
Literature such as Bhoja's works or the Manasollasa
Thinkers Ramanuja and Basaveshwara

questions.q: A historian compares two systems. In the earlier kingdoms, rulers drew tribute from vassals and taxes from traders. Under Muhammad Ghuri, an officer is handed charge of an area for a time and is expected to collect its revenue and keep soldiers ready. What does the chapter say marks the difference?
questions.a: Ghuri's system was more centralised and gave temporary land assignments to officers in return for revenue collection and military service
o: Ghuri's system was more centralised and gave temporary land assignments to officers in return for revenue collection and military service
Ghuri's system left villages to govern themselves, as under the Kakatiyas of Orugallu
Ghuri's system gave officers permanent hereditary kingdoms in return for tribute
Ghuri's system collected revenue only through merchant guilds on the coast

questions.q: A trader plans a cargo with saffron, spices and ginger. (a) From which region does the chapter name each of the three? (b) If seasonal rains failed in the Ganga plains, which crops named for that region would be at risk, and what did many rulers do to soften such failures?
questions.a: (a) Saffron from Kashmir, spices from Kerala, ginger from Bengal. (b) Rice and barley; many rulers took care of irrigation works, which could to some extent mitigate the vagaries of seasonal rains.
s: saffron-Kashmir, spices-Kerala, ginger-Bengal
rice and barley at risk, and irrigation works as the remedy

questions.q: Pooja's teacher describes a 12th-century royal minister at Kalyani who left his post to found a movement that rejected caste distinctions and ritualism, and who wrote short Kannada poems. Whom is she describing?
questions.a: This is Basaveshwara (Basavanna), founder of the Lingayat movement, whose short poems are called vachanas. Ramanuja was a philosopher-saint, Someshvara III a Chalukya king and Jayadeva a Sena court poet.
o: Basaveshwara
Ramanujacharya
Someshvara III
Jayadeva

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Agriculture remained the mainstay of the economy in the 11th and 12th centuries.
Reason (R): India's trade with China and Southeast Asia kept growing in this period.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: (a) Name what a powerful king in this period had to maintain for his army. (b) Why did this make an efficient administration necessary?
questions.a: (a) Soldiers with weapons, and horses and elephants, with camels for transporting provisions in parts of north India. (b) All this needed large resources, so the kingdom had to collect tributes from vassals and taxes from traders efficiently.
s: Part (a): soldiers, weapons, horses, elephants, and camels in the north
Part (b): resources came from tributes of vassals and taxes from traders

questions.q:
Read the following statements about the age.
1. In these two centuries large parts of north India and all of south India remained outside the hold of the Turkic invaders.
2. The Angkor Wat temple in Cambodia was built by the Chola king Rajendra.
3. Merchant guilds survived and adapted despite the disruptions in the north.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 are from the chapter. Statement 2 is false: Angkor Wat was built in the 12th century by the Khmer king Suryavarman II.
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT true of Ramanujacharya, as the chapter describes him?
questions.a: Ramanuja challenged Adi Shankaracharya's advaita vedanta and developed vishishtadvaita vedanta, which emphasises bhakti. The claim that he upheld the advaita school is false.
o: He accepted Shankaracharya's advaita unchanged
He developed the vishishtadvaita school of vedanta
He saw the world and individual souls as real
He stressed bhakti and surrender to the divine

questions.q: An officer in Muhammad Ghuri's system loses his land assignment after some years. (a) Which word in the chapter's description of the system explains this? (b) What two services did he owe in return for the assignment, and what did the chapter say would happen to the system later?
questions.a: (a) 'Temporary': the assignments were temporary. (b) Revenue collection and military service; the system would be developed further during the Delhi Sultanate (Grade 8).
s: the word temporary
revenue collection and military service, and later development under the Delhi Sultanate

questions.q: A guide claims, 'Angkor Wat was built by an Indian dynasty and has nothing in common with Indian temples.' Show with three details from the chapter that this cannot be right.
questions.a: Angkor Wat was built by the Khmer king Suryavarman II, so the first part is wrong. It was first dedicated to Vishnu, with inscriptions in Old Khmer and Sanskrit and bas-reliefs of scenes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata. Its five shikharas symbolise Mount Meru, and it shares many features with south Indian temples, so it has much in common with them.
s: Built by the Khmer king Suryavarman II, not an Indian dynasty
Vishnu dedication, Sanskrit inscriptions and the epics' reliefs
Shares many features with south Indian temples

questions.q: Rahul says, 'The 11th and 12th centuries were mostly about wars and invasions; the only lasting achievements were the temples built by kings.' Do you agree? Give evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Temples are a real achievement: the Chandellas built the Kandariya Mahadeva and Lakshmana temples at Khajuraho, and the Hoysalas their temples. But 'only' is wrong: Bhaskaracharya wrote Lilavati, Someshvara III wrote the Manasollasa, and thinkers such as Ramanuja and Basaveshwara arose.
s: Verdict: partly right
Supports the temple half: Khajuraho or Hoysala temples
Rejects 'only': Lilavati, Manasollasa, or Ramanuja and Basaveshwara

questions.q:
A Delhi school's heritage club has room for one display case on the theme 'How Indian culture travelled to Southeast Asia'. The first candidate is a huge 12th-century temple in Cambodia built by a Khmer king, with inscriptions in two languages, bas-reliefs of two great Indian epics and five towers that stand for a mountain at the centre of the cosmos. The second is a Srivijaya ruler's gift to an Indian university.
(a) Name the temple and its builder.
(b) Name the two languages of its inscriptions and the epics shown.
(c) Name the mountain the five towers symbolise, and the Indian university that received the gift.
(d) Decide which case fits the club's theme better and justify it with two facts; say what the other case shows instead.
questions.a: (a) Angkor Wat, built by Suryavarman II. (b) Old Khmer and Sanskrit; the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. (c) Mount Meru; Nalanda. (d) The Angkor Wat case fits the theme: its Sanskrit inscriptions, Ramayana and Mahabharata reliefs and Vishnu dedication show Indian religious and aesthetic traditions travelling to Southeast Asia, and it shares features with south Indian temples. The Srivijaya gift shows the peaceful cultural relations in the other direction, with Southeast Asia giving to an Indian centre of learning.
s: Part (a): Angkor Wat and Suryavarman II
Part (b): Old Khmer and Sanskrit; Ramayana and Mahabharata
Part (c): Mount Meru; Nalanda
Part (d): Angkor Wat with two facts, and what the Srivijaya gift shows instead

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Basaveshwara's Anubhava Mandapa welcomed men and women from every social, economic, religious and linguistic background.
Reason (R): Basaveshwara looked at the inner value of a person rather than social rank and promoted the equal spiritual potential of all men and women.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true, and the reason explains the assertion: because he valued the inner worth of everyone, he opened the pavilion to people of all backgrounds.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
